To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The Kubo people, who live in a region where bananas are a staple carbohydrate, do not produce bananas in a manner that would make them self-sufficient in their production, but rather in a manner that makes sharing possible."
Kubo people chose to live in a way that was ecologically unsustainable and socially unstable because they were concerned with sorcery.
Bananas were grown by the Kubo to accommodate their needs for sharing, which was a means for managing sorcery."
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the ecological context of food production, the nature of the crop, and the social and political context of production combine to influence the way in which people produce their food.
the ways in which people's social relationships and their ecological knowledge and practice are interlinked.
the way in which people have chosen to live, rather than with the way in the environment has forced them to live, as the dominant theme in human adaptation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Kubo people were not ecological determinists, they were not economic rationalists, they were neither optimisers nor maximisers, they were not even self-interested; they were social beings.
the ecology and community dynamics of the people were mediated through the sharing of bananas.
Kubo people were not self-sufficient in food production, and did not seek to be.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the ecology of the people is important, their social ecology is more so.
the ecology and dynamics of the Kubo people are not to be found in the ecology of their environment but, rather, in the ecology of the social relationships that they have created and maintained.
we are not dealing with a simple, direct relationship between ecology, technology and community.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way people grow crops is not necessarily a reflection of the environment, but rather a response to the social and cultural environment.
the ecology of human societies cannot be understood in isolation from the cultural values and practices that underpin their social and economic organization.
the ecology of human communities is not simply a product of the environment.
